messages.author: 2a7f346506a3e9ff
messages.subject: Parallelization Framework
parts:
Hey,

So I've been working on a little side project implementing parallel tempering (aka replica exchange) in Stan.  Currently I have a functional but non-parallel implementation.  It needs a little testing yet, but it's basically there.

The next step, of course, is to parallelize it.  Unlike running multiple chains, this cannot be done by running multiple independent processes because there are interactions between the running chains.  This leads me to my current question: what do we want to use to parallelize Stan.

Here are the two options as I see it:

1) Threading.  Multiple threads spawned on a single machine using shared memory/locking/etc for communication.

Pros: Convenient when you only have a single machine to run on.  A little easier to work with when parallelization is very simple (like running multiple independent chains or with only simple interactions).
Cons: Cannot distribute across multiple machines.  Getting threading right can sometimes be tricky due to non-threadsafe libraries.

2) MPI.  This is the standard API for distributing across multiple machines.  Communication is done using the MPI interfaces and is done over a network.

Pros: Easy to distribute over any number of cores/machines.  No thread safety issues, as each instance runs as a separate process.
Cons: A little harder to setup sometimes and probably harder than it needs to be for a single machine.  May not work well on Windows as it requires shared file system (I have no experience here though).  A little harder to work with when parallelization is simple but still requires communication (like with parallel tempering).

In both of these cases, there are good boost libraries available to make the code itself cross-platform.

What do people think?  Am I missing something entirely?  Neither of these consider low-level parallelization (things like CUDA, OpenMP, etc) but I think that's a separate discussion.

If left to my own devices, I would probably lean towards an MPI based implementation even though threads might be easier.

Cheers,
Marcus

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] Parallelization Framework
parts:
The decision's usually based on hardware and scalability concerns.

My understanding is that threads (a) are much faster, but (b) only
scale up to the number of cores before throughput begins to go down
rather than up. So if we're targeting one machine, threads seem
like the right choice. They also allow shared memory of the model
more easily if that's an issue.

I don't have experience coding either one in C++.

We'd like to have threads for other purposes, so sorting that
out in Boost would be great. Unlike most of the other Boost
libs, their thread lib is not header only and needs to be compiled
on a per-platform basis.

The only synchronization issue I'm aware of is with auto-dif,
and there's an implementation with thread-local storage (not even
sure if that's available on all platforms yet) that's safe (but
about 15--20% slower in a single thread compared to using regular
storage.

- Bob
